column2: When you are in position, the Pandavas will lose heart, with their ministers, the Panchalas and the Srinjayas.
As the risen sun, shining with its own splendour, dispels dense darkness, so dispel our foes."
[Karna said:] "I said this before, in your presence, O Gandhari's son: I shall conquer the Pandavas, O king, with their sons and with Janardana.
I shall be your commander, there is no doubt of it; be steady, great king, and know the Pandavas as already conquered."
[Sanjaya said:] Thus addressed, King Duryodhana of great splendour rose up with the kings, as Shatakratu with the gods, to honour Karna with the generalship, as the immortals honoured Skanda.
Then, O king, the kings led by Duryodhana, desiring victory, quickly consecrated him with the prescribed rites, with golden and earthen jars consecrated by mantras,
with horns filled with water—of rhinoceros, bull and great ox—with vessels of jewels and pearls, and with other pure and fragrant herbs,
as he sat on a seat of udumbara wood covered with linen, with the rite seen in the scriptures and the accessories well gathered.
Conquer the Parthas with Govinda and their followers in the great battle, the bards and twice-born said to him, O best of the Bharatas.

Slay the Parthas with the Panchalas, Radheya, for our victory, like the sun rising and dispelling darkness with its fierce rays.
mahabharata:8:6.41	The ungrateful Keshavas are unable to bear the arrows loosed by you, as one cannot bear the sight of blazing sunbeams.
mahabharata:8:6.42	The Parthas with the Panchalas cannot stand before you, as danavas cannot before Mahendra with weapons in hand in battle.
Radheya, consecrated, immeasurably splendid in his radiance, outshone all in form, like a second sun.
Your son, having consecrated Radheya as commander, deemed himself fulfilled, driven by time.
Karna too, O king, tamer of foes, having obtained the generalship, ordered the array for the sunrise.
Surrounded by your sons, Karna shone there, O Bharata, like Skanda among the gods in the war with Taraka.
[Dhritarashtra said:] When he had ordered the army to be arrayed, at the sun's rising, what did the greatly wise one do? Tell me that, Sanjaya.
[Sanjaya said:] Knowing Karna's mind, your son, O best of the Bharatas, ordered the array to be formed, with auspicious music and instruments before him.
In the last watch of the night, O revered one, a great sound "Yoga! Yoga!" suddenly arose from your son's camp.
Of elephants being equipped, of armoured chariots, of foot-soldiers arming and of horses, O lord of men,
and of warriors shouting to one another in haste, there arose a tumultuous noise touching the sky.
Then the son of the charioteer appeared with a white banner and horses of the colour of the young sun, a golden-backed bow, an elephant-rope standard,
a quiver full of arrows, armlets, armour, and bearing shataghnis, bells, darts, spears and javelins,
a bow in perfect order, with the lustre of the spotless sun, on a chariot with many banners.
Seeing mighty-bowed Karna on his chariot, best of chariot-warriors, like the rising sun dispelling darkness by thousands of rays,
the Kauravas there, O revered one, did not regard the loss of Bhishma, nor of Drona, nor of others as a calamity, tiger among men.
Then Karna, urging the warriors with the sound of his conch, O revered one, drove forth the Kaurava army.
Having arranged the army in the makara (crocodile) array, the mighty archer, scorcher of foes, then advanced against the Pandavas, desiring victory.
At the mouth of the makara, O king, stood Karna; at its eyes the hero Shakuni and the great chariot-warrior Uluka.
At the head stood Drona's son, at the neck all the uterine brothers, in the middle King Duryodhana surrounded by a great force.
On the left foot, O king of kings, stood Kritavarman, with the Narayana forces and herdsmen, arrogant in battle.
On the right foot, O king, stood Gautama (Kripa) of true prowess, surrounded by Trigartas, mighty archers and southerners.
On the left hind foot stood Shalya with a great army arisen from the Madra country.
On the right, O great king, stood Sushena, true to his word, surrounded by thousands of chariots and hundreds of elephants.
At the tail stood the two great-hearted royal brothers Chitrasena and Chitra with a great army.
When Karna, the best of men, had advanced, O king of kings, the king of dharma, looking at Dhananjaya, said this:

See, Partha, the great army of Dhritarashtra's son in the battle, arrayed by Karna, hero, guarded by heroic great chariot-warriors.
mahabharata:8:7.24	This great host of Dhritarashtra's son has been stripped of its heroes; little remains, mighty-armed one, and I count it as straw.
mahabharata:8:7.25	Here only one mighty archer stands, the charioteer's son, who is unconquerable by gods, asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras and great serpents, and by the three worlds of moving and unmoving beings, best of chariot-warriors.
mahabharata:8:7.26	Having slain him today, mighty-armed one, the victory will be yours, Phalguna, and the thorn of my twelve years will be pulled out. Knowing this, mighty-armed one, arrange the array as you wish.
Hearing his brother's words, the white-horsed Pandava countered that army with the half-moon array.
On the left stood Bhimasena, O king, and on the right the mighty archer Dhrishtadyumna of great strength.
In the middle of the array was the Pandava himself with Krishna as charioteer; Nakula, Sahadeva and the king of dharma were behind.
The two Panchalas Yudhamanyu and Uttamaujas, guarding the wheels, did not leave Arjuna in battle, being protected by Kiritin.
The remaining brave kings stood in the array armoured, each according to feeling, zeal and strength, O Bharata.
Having thus arrayed that great formation, O Bharata, the Pandavas and your mighty archers set their minds on battle.
Seeing your army arrayed by the charioteer's son in the battle, your son with his kin thought the Pandavas slain.
Likewise Yudhishthira, seeing the Pandava army arrayed, thought Dhritarashtra's sons with Karna slain, O lord of men.
Then conches, kettledrums, tabors, anakas and cow-horns suddenly sounded, and noises arose on all sides.
On both armies, O king, great sounds were played, and the lion-roar of heroes eager for victory arose.
The neighing of horses, the trumpeting of elephants and the fierce rattle of chariot wheels arose, O lord of men.
No one knew the grief for Drona, O best of the Bharatas, on seeing mighty-bowed Karna armoured at the front of the array.
The two great armies, of great strength, with delighted men and elephants, stood eager to fight, O king, to strike each other at once.
There, intent and greatly enraged, standing facing one another, Karna and the Pandava shone in the midst of the armies, O king of kings.
The two armies, as if dancing, met each other; those eager to fight went out from their flanks and counter-flanks.
Then the battle began of men, elephants, horses and chariot-warriors, O great king, each fiercely striking the other.
Then elephants, chariots, horses and foot-soldiers in the great battle engaged in a supreme combat that destroyed sin, O lord.
With heads of lion-like men, equal in beauty and fragrance to the full moon, sun and lotuses, lion-like men strewed the earth.
With half-moon arrows, spears, razor-edged arrows, swords, pattishas and axes they cut off the heads of the fighters.
Long arms were severed by long arms; arms with fists cut off, still bearing weapons and armlets, fell.
Those quivering arms with bloody fingers shone on the earth like five-headed serpents struck down by Garuda.
Heroes struck by their foes fell from horses, chariots and elephants, like the dwellers in heaven falling from celestial cars when their merit is exhausted.
Struck down by maces, other heavy iron clubs, and pestles, hundreds of heroes fell in battle at the hands of stronger heroes.
Chariots were smashed by chariots, rutting elephants by rutting elephants, horsemen by horsemen in that dense crush.
Chariots by better chariots and elephants, horsemen by foot-soldiers, foot-soldiers by horsemen, lay slain in the battle.
Chariots, horses and infantry by elephants; elephants and infantry by chariots; chariots, infantry and elephants by horses; and horses, chariots and elephants by men,
made a great slaughter of chariots, horses, elephants and men, with hands, feet, weapons and chariots.
While our army was being slain by heroes in that battle, the Parthas led by Vrikodara advanced against us.
Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandin, the sons of Draupadi, the Prabhadrakas, Satyaki and Chekitana, with Dravidian soldiers,
hired with great wealth, the Pandyas, Chodas and Keralas, broad-chested, long-armed, tall and handsome,
pressing, red-toothed, with the prowess of rutting elephants, in garments of various hues, dusted with scented powders,
with swords bound on, nooses in hand, a match for elephants and counter-elephants, destined to die alike, O king, standing in their ranks against each other,
with quivers, bows in hand, long-haired, loving battle—Satyaki's foot-soldiers, the Andhras, of dreadful form and prowess.
Then others again, brave warriors, the Chedis, Panchalas, Kekayas, Karushas, Kosalas, Kashis and Magadhas, rushed forward.
Their chariots, elephants, excellent horses and infantry, delighted, danced and laughed with sounds of many kinds.
Surrounded by the best of great ministers, Vrikodara came to the middle of that great army, mounted on an elephant, towards your force.
That excellent elephant, extremely fierce and duly equipped, shone like the sun risen over the best house on the eastern mountain.
Its excellent iron armour, adorned with the finest jewels, was of the brilliance of the autumn sky dotted with stars.
He, with javelin and spear in hand, with a beautiful diadem, richly adorned, moving about like the midday sun, burnt his foes with his splendour.
Seeing that elephant from afar, Kshemadhurti, seated on an elephant, challenging, rushed upon him with delight at one who was even more delighted.
A fierce battle took place between those two elephants, like that of two great mountains with trees, by chance.
Their elephants locked together, the two heroes, piercing each other with javelins bright as sunbeams, roared.
Drawing back, the two elephants moved in circles, and the heroes, taking up their bows, struck each other.
With shouts and the slapping of arms and twanging of arrows on all sides, the two heroes delighted the men and uttered lion-roars.
The two skilful, mighty fighters, on elephants with raised trunks and banners fluttering in the wind, fought each other.
Cutting each other's bows, they roared at each other and rained darts and javelins like two clouds pouring water in the rains.
Kshemadhurti then pierced Bhima in the chest with a javelin, with force, roaring, and with six others besides.
Bhimasena, with javelins lodged in his body and his frame blazing with anger, shone like the sun with seven horses surrounded by clouds.
Then Bhima, with effort, hurled at his foe a javelin of the colour of the sun, swift and straight.
Then the lord of the Kuluta, drawing his bow, cut the javelin with ten arrows and pierced the Pandava with a dart.
Then the Pandava, taking up a bow that sounded like a great cloud, tormented the enemy's elephant with arrows, in a rage.
Tormented by the shower of arrows from Bhimasena in battle, that elephant, being restrained, could not stand, like a cloud scattered by the wind.
The king of elephants of Bhimasena rushed at that elephant, like a cloud driven by a great wind rushing at another.
Turning his elephant back with effort, Kshemadhurti pierced with arrows Bhimasena's charging elephant.
Then the bull among men, with a well-loosed razor-arrow, cut his enemy's bow and tormented the hostile elephant.
Then Kshemadhurti struck Bhima with a lance and killed his elephant with iron arrows in all its vital parts.
Leaping to the ground before his elephant fell, Bhimasena crushed the enemy's elephant with his mace.
As Kshemadhurti ran from the crushed elephant towards him with a raised sword, Vrikodara struck him with his mace.
He fell dead with his sword, lifeless beside his elephant, like a lion struck by a thunderbolt beside a mountain shattered by it.
Seeing the renowned king of the Kulutas slain, your army, distressed, fled, O best of the Bharatas.
So too the Pandavas, O king, enraged, the great chariot-warriors, slew your son's army at Karna's front.
Karna, O king, the mighty-armed, destroyed the Pandava army with iron arrows polished by smiths and bright as sunbeams.
There, O Bharata, elephants struck by Karna's arrows roared, collapsed, grew faint and wandered in all ten directions.
While that army was being slain by the charioteer's son, O revered one, Nakula quickly rushed at the charioteer's son in the great battle.
Bhimasena confronted Drona's son, who was doing difficult deeds; Satyaki held back Vinda and Anuvinda, the Kekayas.
King Chitrasena confronted the oncoming Shrutakarman, and Chitra, with banner and bow, confronted Pratívindhya.
Duryodhana attacked King Yudhishthira, son of Dharma; Dhananjaya, enraged, attacked the Samshaptaka bands.
In that slaughter of great heroes, Dhrishtadyumna met Kripa; Shikhandin met the unfallen Kritavarman.
Shrutakirti met Shalya, and the valiant Sahadeva, son of Madri, met your son Duhshasana, O great king.
In battle Satyaki covered the two Kekayas with a shining rain of arrows, and the two Kekayas covered Satyaki, O Bharata.
Those two Bharata heroes struck him hard in the breast, as elephants strike a counter-elephant with their tusks in a great fight.
With their armour pierced by arrows, those two brothers in battle struck Satyaki, true in his deeds, with arrows, O king.
Satyaki, laughing, O great king, covered them on every side with a rain of arrows and held them back, O Bharata.
Held back by the showers of Shaineya's arrows, the two quickly covered Shaineya's chariot with arrows.
Shauri (Satyaki) cut their variegated bows in the great fight and covered them with sharp, irresistible arrows.
Then the two took other polished bows and great arrows, and swiftly and skilfully filled Satyaki with arrows as they moved.
Great arrows loosed by them, feathered with heron plumes and adorned with gold, lighting up all directions, flew in all directions.
A darkness of arrows arose, O king, in the great fight between them, and those great chariot-warriors cut each other's bows.
Then enraged, O great king, the Satvata, arrogant in battle, taking another bow and stringing it, cut off Anuvinda's head with a very sharp razor-headed arrow.
That head, pressed by its earrings, fell to the ground like the head of Shambara slain in the great battle, and the dead Kekaya brought grief to all the Kekayas as it went swiftly to earth.
Seeing that hero slain, his brother, a great chariot-warrior, took another strung bow and held Shaineya back.
Having pierced Satyaki with a dart and arrows with golden shafts sharpened on stone, he roared mightily and said, "Stand, stand!"
Again the enraged great chariot-warrior of the Kekayas tormented Satyaki's arms and chest with arrows like tongues of fire.
That Satvata, knowing true valour, his whole body wounded by arrows, shone in battle, O king, like a flowering kimshuka tree.
Pierced in battle by the great-souled Kekaya, Satyaki pierced the Kekaya with twenty-five arrows, as if laughing.
Taking up shields marked with a hundred moons and swords, those two strong-armed men shone in the great arena like Jambha and Shakra, mighty ones, in the war of gods and asuras.
Then those two, moving in circles in the great battle, quickly struck each other with swords in the fight.
The Satvata cut the Kekaya's shield in two, and that king likewise cut Satyaki's shield.
Having cut Satyaki's shield, the Kaikeya moved in circles, forwards and backwards, amid a hundred groups of stars.
As he moved in the great arena wielding his excellent sword, Shaineya swiftly cut him in two with a sidelong stroke.
That Kekaya king, in armour, cut in two in the great fight, fell, mighty archer, like a mountain struck by thunder.
Having slain him in battle, the hero Shaineya, best of charioteers, scorcher of foes, quickly mounted the chariot of Yudhamanyu.
Then, mounting another chariot duly equipped, Satyaki again destroyed the great army of the Kekayas with arrows.
That great Kekaya army, being slain in battle, abandoned him and fled in all ten directions.
The king Abhisara struck Shrutakarman with nine sharp arrows and pierced his charioteer with five.
Then Shrutakarman, enraged, at the head of the army tormented Chitrasena in a vital spot with a very sharp iron arrow.
In the meantime the greatly renowned Shrutakirti covered that protector of the earth with ninety feathered arrows.
Regaining consciousness, the great chariot-warrior Chitrasena cut his bow with a broad-headed arrow and pierced him with seven.
Taking another bow, gold-adorned and swift, he made Chitrasena more variegated with waves of arrows.
O king, stuck with arrows, the youth, wearing a garland of many colours, shone like a young man richly adorned in the midst of an assembly.
Then in the battle, enraged, he pierced Shrutakarman in the chest with an iron arrow and said, "Stand, stand!"
Shrutakarman too, tormented in battle by the iron arrow, streamed much blood, like a mountain with streams of red ochre.
Then, O king, Shrutakarman, assailed by his foes, protecting himself against enemies, cut his bow in two.
Then Shrutakarman of great renown, best of the Bharatas, pierced him, whose bow was cut, with three hundred iron arrows.
Then with another very sharp broad-headed arrow he quickly struck off the head and helmet of that great soul.
That great head of Chitravarman fell to the ground, as if by chance the moon had fallen from heaven to earth.
Seeing the king and Abhisara slain, O revered one, Chitrasena's soldiers rushed forward swiftly.
Then the enraged mighty archer routed that army with arrows; Shrutakarman shone, quickly driving them with arrows as Yama, lord of the dead, enraged at the end of time drives all beings.
Then Pratívindhya pierced Chitra with five swift arrows, struck his charioteer with three, and his banner with one arrow.
Chitra tormented his arms and chest with nine broad-headed arrows, golden-shafted, whetted on stone, and feathered with heron plumes.
Pratívindhya, O Bharata, cut his bow with arrows and struck him with five sharp shafts.
Then, O great king, Chitra hurled at your son a terrible, hard-to-resist dart with a golden shaft, like a tongue of fire.
As that dart came suddenly like a meteor from the sky, Pratívindhya cut it in two in battle, as if laughing.
Cut by Pratívindhya's sharp arrows, it fell, terrifying all beings like a thunderbolt at the end of an age.
Seeing that dart destroyed, Chitra took up a great mace adorned with a golden net and hurled it at Pratívindhya.
It killed his horses and his charioteer in the great battle, crushed the chariot and swiftly fell to the earth.
At that very moment, O Bharata, leaping from his chariot, Pratívindhya hurled at Chitra a dart adorned with golden bells.
Chitra, high-minded, caught that falling dart, O king, and hurled that very dart back at Pratívindhya, O Bharata.
Reaching the hero Pratívindhya in battle, the splendid dart pierced his right arm and fell to the ground, lighting up the spot like a thunderbolt.
Then, O king, Pratívindhya, greatly enraged, hurled a gold-adorned javelin desiring Chitra's death.
It pierced his divine armour and his heart, and swiftly entered the earth like a great serpent into its hole.
Struck by the javelin, he fell then, O king, stretching out his two broad, plump arms like iron bars.
Seeing Chitra slain, your warriors, resplendent in battle, rushed swiftly at Pratívindhya from all sides.
Letting fly arrows of many kinds and shataghnis with bells, they covered him as banks of clouds cover the sun.
The mighty-armed one, repelling them with a net of arrows in battle, routed your army as the thunderbolt-wielder routed the asura host.
Slain in battle by the Pandavas, O king, your men were suddenly scattered like clouds driven by the wind.
While that army fled, being slain on every side, Drona's son alone swiftly advanced against mighty Bhimasena.
Then a dreadful encounter suddenly took place between the two, as in the war of gods and asuras between Vritra and Vasava.
Then he struck him again with ninety sharp arrows, seeing all his vital points, like one knowing vital points and quick of hand.
Bhimasena, covered with sharp arrows by Drona's son, shone in battle, O king, like the radiant sun.
[Vaishampayana said:] Then, when Karna was slain, O king, Suyodhana, Dhritarashtra's son, sunk in an ocean of grief, became hopeless on all sides.
Sighing long and hot, they thought of the Pandavas, and hearing the dreadful roar of the Pandavas eager for victory,
[Vaishampayana said:] his hundred sons slain, the king Dhritarashtra, wretched like a tree with severed branches, tormented with grief for his sons,
Dvaipayana, Narada, Devala, the great sage Devasthana, Kanva, and their excellent disciples,
Seeing you, tiger among men, with your limbs drenched in blood and streaming like a mountain, I sink like a lotus in the rains.
The Pandavas, O king, saw the righteous Yudhishthira distressed, fallen on the ground, sighing again and again.
[Vaishampayana said:] Having regained the kingdom and slain their enemies, the great-souled Pandavas ruled the earth with Dhritarashtra before them.
These and many other portents, fearful and causing distress to the heart, were shown day after day, O king.
Thus addressed, the valiant son of Kunti, saying "Time, time," accepted that word of his eldest brother.
Having attained heaven, the third realm, Yudhishthira, king of dharma, saw Duryodhana seated on a throne, endowed with glory.
